title: The City paid more than the organization says it took in
question: In which years does the City's ledger show more money paid to an organization than the organization's own tax return reports as its entire revenue, or its entire spending, for the matching year?
finding: Across 2,001 organization-years in which the City paid 463 organizations $100,000 or more, 12 organizations had at least one year in which City payments alone exceeded the total revenue on the organization's own tax return, by $28.6 million in their worst years combined; the largest is San Francisco Public Health Foundation, paid $13.5 million in the tax year ended 30 June 2022 against reported revenue of $1.6 million. For 7 of them the City's payments exceed reported revenue over every year on file added together, for 2 the gap is covered by a fall in money owed to them on their own balance sheet, and for 3 the return offers no clue to the reason. A further 9 organizations reported enough revenue but spent less in total than the City alone paid. 21 other one-year gaps disappeared when the year was pooled with its neighbour and are not listed.
how: City money is every payment to the organization in the Controller's table of all City payments (Vendor Payments), under any payee spelling tied to its employer number, by the fiscal year printed on the payment, except payments that table labels as loans, as money held for a benefit district, as benefit-plan payments from a trust fund or as debt service. Alignment rule: each City fiscal year (July to June) is spread onto the organization's tax year by days of overlap, so a June year-end matches one fiscal year and a December year-end takes half of each of two. A year is listed only if City payments were at least $100,000, exceeded total revenue (or total expenses) on the return by $25,000 and 2%, and still exceeded it when the year was pooled with the return before and, separately, with the return after. The second gap column restates revenue to money received, using the return's own balance sheet: a fall in money owed to the organization and a rise in payments received in advance are added. One row per organization, showing its largest gap; rows are ordered by the gap that survives that restatement.
limits: The City records a payment when it is made; the return records revenue when earned, in the organization's own year. The pooling test removes most timing shifts but not a long delay. A parent may be paid for work its affiliates report; a fiscal sponsor or agent may hold money that is not its revenue; a multi-year grant can be booked in one year; a loan or money for a building is not revenue at all; and merged or renamed bodies can file under another number. The last column names whichever of these the return itself points to. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. For 23 of the 485 organizations matched here that makes the City figure at least $1 million and 10% higher over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $1.36 billion higher in all. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. A return may not count money that passes through as revenue. For the organizations matched here, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $425.1 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (14 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. Organizations are matched to tax returns by payee name and employer number; a wrong match would create a false gap. A gap is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.

rows.pattern: More than all the revenue it reported
rows.clue: Fiscal sponsorship or pass-through: the return describes such work, and money held for others can be booked outside revenue. Explained by its audit: it books fiscal-sponsor inflows ($23,637,451 that year) as a liability, not revenue, and the City's payment fits inside them.

rows.pattern: More than all the revenue it reported
rows.clue: The return gives no clue. Of the $75.1 million counted as City money for it here over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $32.0 million is not in the Controller's nonprofit-spending table. The largest group of those payment lines ($32.0 million) is labelled “Materials & Supplies; Food” in the payment file, mostly under the contract titles “HSA COVID-19 Great Plates” and “HSA COVID-19: Meal Services”. Such money can be aid passing through to others rather than payment for the organization's own work. Either way it is a real City payment.
